label: GPT-6 Astra
output:
Peter, nine years running payroll is not something I would dismiss. You’re right about the risks of people borrowing against every payday, the difficulty of recovering money from leavers, and the amount of time an informal scheme can swallow. Brenda’s current arrangement, where someone comes to her office and a supervisor agrees, needs to change.

Where I disagree quite strongly is the idea that you close the window, give people some financial education, and after one or two difficult pay cycles they adjust. We tried almost exactly that in 2025. We ended up reversing it.

I’m in logistics, with roughly 340 staff, mostly drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks. We closed salary advances in February 2025 after Finance raised much the same objections you have: we are not a bank, advances complicate cash flow, and some employees were coming back every month. We gave two months’ notice rather than your suggested three, and held a financial literacy session with the SACCO.

On paper, we had stopped a problem. In practice, some of the problem moved out of payroll and into other departments.

In the six months after closure, reception logged **61 debt collector or loan-app calls**, up from a handful before. Some apps were also contacting supervisors whom employees had listed as referees. So while I agree that the loan is the employee’s own contract, the consequences did not stay neatly between the employee and the lender. Reception was fielding calls. Supervisors were being dragged into collection conversations. Staff were trying to sort out debts during working hours.

We also saw an increase in unplanned absence on the two days after month-end. Our fleet manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers who were “sorting out” loans.

I want to be careful about that point. We cannot prove that every absence, or every one of those calls, was caused by closing advances. This was not a controlled study. But those were actual operational issues arising during the period when we had supposedly removed the cost and distraction of lending to staff. They deserved to be counted alongside the payroll time we had saved.

One loader at Changamwe had six apps on the go by the time he came to me, borrowing from one to repay another. It took four months of work with payroll to unwind that situation. I cannot say that keeping advances would have prevented all of it. I can say that closing our scheme did not mean we stopped spending HR and payroll time on employees’ borrowing.

That is why “they always adjust” does not match our experience. Some do adjust. Others borrow somewhere more expensive and spend the next few months trying to keep up.

The SACCO is useful, and we still encourage it. But our SACCO loans take two to three weeks and require guarantors. That is not an answer to a child being sent home from school over fees on a Tuesday. It may be a good answer to a planned expense; it is not always a workable answer to an immediate one.

Financial literacy is useful too. I would not scrap that either. But on KES 28,000 a month, knowing how to budget and having enough money to absorb an emergency are two different things. We should help people plan without assuming that every shortfall is a failure to plan.

We reopened advances in September 2025, but we did **not** bring back the old informal arrangement. We introduced a written policy:

- **Maximum advance: 40% of net pay**, subject to the deduction checks.
- **Once per pay cycle**, with no additional top-ups.
- **Repaid in full at the next payroll**, rather than rolled over.
- **No fee.**
- **Requests through the payroll portal**, not a queue outside my office.

We also check existing deductions before approving anything. The Employment Act limits total deductions to two-thirds of wages, and an advance request does not override that limit. The 40% cap is a maximum, not an automatic entitlement regardless of what someone already owes. Nobody should reach month-end and discover that we have left them with nothing.

Since reopening, we have been handling about 55–70 requests a month, averaging around KES 9,000 each. Recovery has been 100% apart from two leavers; the total written off was roughly KES 14,000 for the year.

So your point about leavers is valid. We did lose money. I would put that figure in front of Finance, not hide it. But I would also put it next to the time spent dealing with collection calls, the absence, the missed runs and the months spent untangling a debt problem. The advance write-off is easy to see in an account. The other costs are spread across reception, HR, payroll and operations, which makes them easier to overlook.

For cash-flow purposes, our current volumes represent roughly KES 495,000–630,000 being paid early in a typical month. That is not a trivial amount, and Finance is entitled to plan for it. But it is an early payment recovered at payroll, not the same thing as an expense or a write-off.

Our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself. What changed his mind was having written limits and a forecastable exposure rather than requests arriving as surprises. He can work with a ceiling. The old arrangement gave him very little to work with.

I also agree with you that repeat borrowing deserves attention. We have not proved that a salary advance solves someone’s underlying financial difficulties. It doesn’t. Someone requesting the maximum every cycle may need a separate conversation and support. But I would rather identify that pattern through payroll than discover it when a collector starts ringing their supervisor.

Brenda, for the meeting on the 18th, I would not defend the scheme exactly as it stands. Your Finance Manager has a reasonable objection to an arrangement with no written limit and no consistent process. I would propose replacing it, rather than choosing between keeping everything informal and stopping everything.

Take the shape of a policy: a net-pay cap, once per cycle, full recovery at the next payroll, a defined approval route through payroll, and checks against existing deductions and the statutory limit. Agree who authorises requests and how Finance will see the expected cash requirement. You could propose a time-limited trial with a review date rather than ask for an indefinite commitment.

Then take your own numbers: how many advances you currently pay, their average value, how many people request them repeatedly, what has actually gone unrecovered, and how much staff time administration takes. Ask operations about any debt-related disruption too, without assuming every absence is about money. Our figures are an example, not a forecast for your workforce.

Peter, I think we agree that HR should not be running an informal lending desk. Where we differ is whether stopping advances necessarily gets the employer out of the problem. For us, it didn’t. Written rules and limits turned out to be more manageable than either the old open-ended scheme or a complete ban.
